name: Pentapeptide-18

lead: Pentapeptide-18 is a short peptide marketed as Leuphasyl for fine expression lines, often described as a topical, 'Botox-like' ingredient.
Published work is mostly formulation and cell studies; the one human study used a cream that also contained retinol.

paras: It is described as an enkephalin mimic that binds receptors at nerve endings, closing calcium channels and reducing acetylcholine release, though the cited papers did not directly test this in skin.
No peptide-specific adverse events were found in the sources; retinol in the studied cream was linked to extra peeling. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

lead: Pentapeptide-18 (Tyr-D-Ala-Gly-Phe-Leu), sold by supplier Lipotec as Leuphasyl, is a cosmetic peptide marketed to soften expression lines. Papers describe it as an enkephalin mimic that is proposed to bind enkephalin receptors on nerve endings, close calcium channels and reduce acetylcholine release, a mechanism sometimes called 'Botox-like' [1][2].

Published evidence on the peptide alone is sparse. A 2024 study of a retinol-and-pentapeptide-18 eye cream reported wrinkle-area reductions in 20 women, but the cream's effect cannot be separated from retinol [1]. Research on the peptide itself consists largely of formulation and in vitro work [1][2].

paras: The 2024 paper links the peptide to SNAP-25 and the SNARE complex and says it acts like enkephalins at neuromuscular synapses [1]. It states that clinical studies have confirmed anti-wrinkle effects but supports this only with a review and a supplier brochure [1]. A 2020 paper calls it a neurotransmitter inhibitor and notes that its own work did not test the anti-wrinkle mechanism [2].

In an uncontrolled-design report, 20 women aged 30 to 65 used a night eye cream containing retinol and pentapeptide-18 in solid lipid nanoparticles, or the base cream, for 8 weeks. The nanoparticle cream was associated with a 20 percent reduction in total wrinkle area versus 11 percent for the base, with smaller changes in hydration and elasticity [1]. The study did not randomize or blind and the peptide's contribution could not be isolated; authors were connected to the cream's manufacturer [1].
No trial of pentapeptide-18 alone in people was found.

A 2020 study added D-tyrosine to the peptide's ends and found the modified versions reduced melanin and tyrosinase activity in melanocytes and a 3D skin model, an in vitro result about modified peptides, not the commercial one [2]. A 2024 study examined retinol and oligopeptide lipid nanocarriers for anti-acne and anti-aging use [3].
